facts.raw_span: A man in his 60s developed asthenia, anorexia, and cough
Six days later, he was hospitalized with diffuse bilateral pneumonia
Numerous 3- to 6-mm pseudovesicular papules with superficial crusting were noted on the trunk
The papules were asymptomatic
Within 48 hours the papules evolved to an extensive, but not confluent, purpuric rash

Nasopharyngeal swab using real-time reverse transcriptase–polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) - Diagnostic testing on superficial skin sample for herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and SARS-CoV-2 viruses (all negative)
Immunohistochemical testing for herpes simplex and varicella zoster viruses (negative)
RT-PCR testing of fixed skin tissue for SARS-CoV-2 (negative)
Histologic analysis showed: - Extensive epidermal necrosis with acantholysis
Large multinucleated keratinocytes with ballooning degeneration
Dense perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with extravasated erythrocytes and eosinophils in superficial dermis
Early-stage vasculitic alterations with endothelial swelling of dermal vessels without fibrinoid necrosis or thrombosis

concepts.why: The patient's presentation of pseudovesicular papules with superficial crusting and subsequent purpuric rash is consistent with varicella-zoster virus infection, although the negative diagnostic tests make this less likely.
The histologic analysis showing early-stage vasculitic alterations with endothelial swelling of dermal vessels supports the diagnosis of vasculitis.
The extensive epidermal necrosis with acantholysis and large multinucleated keratinocytes with ballooning degeneration are characteristic of toxic epidermal necrolysis.
The patient's presentation of pseudovesicular papules, purpuric rash, and histologic findings of epidermal necrosis are consistent with Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

The patient's presentation of pseudovesicular papules and purpuric rash could be consistent with parvovirus B19 infection, although this diagnosis is less likely given the lack of specific diagnostic testing.
The patient's presentation of pseudovesicular papules and purpuric rash could be consistent with a drug-induced rash, although the specific culprit drug is not identified.
The patient's presentation of asthenia, anorexia, and cough could be consistent with infectious mononucleosis, although the lack of specific diagnostic testing makes this diagnosis less likely.
The patient's presentation of diffuse bilateral pneumonia is consistent with pneumonia, although the specific cause is not identified.
